nodes.label: Article XXII — The system reveals its own weaknesses
Stage 26 — Capacity: seeding, profiling, and the pages that scan (planned, half built)
nodes.rationale: Status is in progress, not implemented: bench:seed, bench:report, the profiling harness, batched scoring, scores:prune, the tally index, a bounded /weaknesses and the load test are in; the acceptance run at 100,000 claims and the run against a real droplet are not. Nothing here changes what the ledger records or how a claim is scored — only how much of the graph a request touches.

nodes.label: The three ceilings: /weaknesses, claim_scores, and serialised writes
nodes.rationale: The failure is not storage or signatures. /weaknesses walks the whole graph and scores every claim under every released model (~36 ms a claim, unusable at 10,000); claim_scores is keyed on an exact seq and never pruned, so the cache already outweighs the log; and Ledger::Append's pg_advisory_xact_lock is a global write ceiling (~31/s) — correct, and it stays, because it is what makes the sequence gap-free and the chain unbroken.

nodes.label: The score cache is an N+1 and was 70% of the report
nodes.rationale: Scoring::Score.call opened with a find_by per claim per model — about 6,000 round trips for a whole-graph report, nearly all missing because the head seq moves with every append. The report paid a query to learn nothing, then computed anyway. Scoring::Score.call_many asks the cache once for the whole set; the computation is untouched and the spec asserts the trace and its hash are byte-identical to scoring one claim at a time (Invariant 4).

nodes.label: A score cache may be discarded because a score is a pure function of the log
nodes.rationale: scores:prune keeps the head seq, every pinned snapshot and anything within KEEP_DAYS. Nothing epistemic is lost: a pruned row returns byte-identical, which is the only reason a cache may be thrown away at all, and the spec deletes the head's rows and rescoring to prove it.

nodes.label: An expression index on the envelope, not a denormalised column on the log
nodes.rationale: Contributors::Tally joins contributions to agent_delegations through envelope->>'delegation_id', which nothing indexed, so crediting an agent's work to its principal scanned the log. The delegation id lives inside the signed envelope, and denormalising it would add a column to the one table this project is most careful about. Measured cost to writes: none detectable.

nodes.label: Two recorded departures: bench:rss instead of derailed_benchmarks, pg_stat_statements deferred
nodes.rationale: derailed_benchmarks would have brought a dependency tree, a second way of booting the app and its own idea of a request, to answer a question /proc/self/status answers in twenty lines — and the twenty lines let the slope be taken over the second half of a run, which is what makes the number honest. pg_stat_statements needed a shared_preload_libraries change and a restart; without query-level attribution a load test produces numbers nobody can attribute, so it must be closed before the load test, not after.

nodes.label: Bench::Isolation — measuring the app, not the reloader
nodes.rationale: The reloader, verbose query logs and log writes were a fifth of the samples in the first profile and none of them exists in production. Profiling also swaps the page cache for a null store, so a page that caches its own answer is measured doing the work rather than reading yesterday's. A timing without the corpus and machine it was taken on is not evidence, so every run is written up under docs/profiler/.
